name: Osmotic Cranial Pressure Induction Rifle OCPIR-3 'Headwater'
description:
The OCPIR-3 operates by projecting a tightly focused beam of modulated osmotic-induction radiation that penetrates the skull and disrupts the choroid plexus — the brain tissue responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid. The beam artificially accelerates CSF production while simultaneously inducing localized vasoconstriction in the arachnoid granulations, blocking the fluid's reabsorption pathway. Within seconds, intracranial pressure begins to climb, causing escalating symptoms ranging from blinding headache and visual distortion to projectile vomiting and loss of motor control. At sustained exposure, the effect becomes life-threatening.

What distinguishes the Headwater from cruder neural-targeting weapons is its precision gradient control. Operators can dial the induction intensity to achieve calibrated non-lethal incapacitation — a target left writhing but intact — or ramp the beam to levels that risk cerebral herniation. This tunability made it enormously attractive to corporate security contractors who needed a weapon that could be justified in court as 'non-lethal deployment' while still carrying the implicit threat of a lethal setting.

The weapon is built on a long-barreled platform resembling an anti-materiel rifle, fitted with a large-aperture emitter dish that gives it an unmistakable silhouette. Users report that targets struck at mid-range settings describe the experience as 'the worst migraine of my life followed by not knowing where my legs were.' Street medics in GLMZ's lower tiers have learned to recognize the presentation and carry emergency hypertonic saline kits as a field countermeasure.
specifications:
effective range: 8–120 meters
beam aperture: 14 cm dish emitter
pressure induction range: 5–42 mmHg above baseline ICP
time to incapacitation: 4–18 seconds depending on intensity setting
power source: High-density osmotic-induction cell, 28 discharges per cell
weight: 6.1 kg
length: 112 cm
intensity settings: 9 graduated levels (1 = discomfort, 9 = herniation risk)
cooldown between shots: 3.2 seconds
tactical_use: Used primarily for crowd control of high-value targets where conventional weapons would cause unacceptable property damage or media optics. Security teams deploy it to collapse a single individual in a group without alerting bystanders to the method. Hostage negotiators in corporate extraction ops use it to silently incapacitate a target holding a dead-man switch. At lethal settings, it has seen use as an assassination tool — the resulting death mimics hypertensive crisis, complicating forensic attribution.
cultural_context: The Headwater has a particularly dark reputation in GLMZ's activist and journalist communities. Several high-profile whistleblowers have died of 'sudden intracranial hemorrhage' within days of publishing damaging corporate data, and the weapon is strongly suspected in at least four cases. The phrase 'getting headwatered' has entered street slang to mean being silently neutralized by institutional power — whether by the weapon specifically or by any invisible, deniable force. Carrying one marks a person as either corporate enforcement or extremely well-connected black market. Civilians who acquire them do so almost exclusively for status.
known_users: HELIX BIOSYSTEMS internal security division 'Meridian Wellness Enforcement'
Fixer 'Constance Vael' — known for non-lethal contract fulfillment
story_hooks: A series of deaths ruled as natural hypertensive events are actually a coordinated Headwater assassination campaign — the party must find the shooter before the next target, a protected witness, is killed.
A black market OCPIR-3 is found locked to a specific biometric — whoever it's keyed to can never be identified because the weapon's registration has been scrubbed. Who was it built to kill?
A street medic begins stockpiling the antidote kits in a specific district — she knows something is coming, but won't say what.

A corporate lawyer argues in open court that the Headwater's 'non-lethal' classification means its use against protestors was lawful. The party is hired by the families — or by the corporation — to shape the outcome.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, purpose-built rifle with an oversized hemispherical emitter dish dominating the muzzle. The overall silhouette evokes an anti-materiel platform — long, angular, predatory — but the dish's organic curve and the absence of any traditional barrel breach create an unsettling asymmetry. It reads as medical precision weaponized.
physical_description.dimensions: Length: 112 cm. Emitter dish diameter: 14 cm. Receiver depth: 8 cm. Stock-to-trigger: 38 cm.
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty but balanced. The 6.1 kg load distributes forward into the dish, creating a front-heavy feel that demands braced shooting. Shoulder-mounted or bipod-mounted; unsustainable in unsupported aim for more than 10 seconds.
physical_description.primary_material: Titanium-alloy receiver and barrel housing. The emitter dish is a monocrystalline sapphire composite with embedded osmotic-induction coils visible through translucent sections.
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal gray receiver with brushed titanium accents. The sapphire dish has a faint opalescent sheen under light, shifting faintly blue-to-violet as internal power states cycle. All edges beveled and polished — clinical, not tactical.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal and brushed steel primary. Accent stripes in surgical blue along the action rails. The emitter dish interior glows faintly with violet undertones when charged. Helix Biosystems' circular molecular logo inlaid in chrome on the left side of the receiver.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer grip with faint ergonomic dimpling. Cool to the touch. A rubberized palm swell near the trigger guard is wrapped in a thin synthetic cord in the same surgical blue as the accent stripes — prevents slippage when wet or bloodied.
distinctive_features: Large hemispherical sapphire emitter dish with visible coil matrices beneath surface
Digital intensity readout (LED numerals 1–9) mounted on top rail, cycling faintly in sleep mode
Twin thermal vents along the receiver sides — radiating subtle heat even when idle
A recessed secondary aiming port (laser-sighted) below the main optics rail for mid-range precision
Cooldown indicator light (red → amber → green) below the charging receptacle
Faint etching around the dish rim denoting safety certification and intracranial pressure threshold warnings
Osmotic-induction cell port (thumb-release clip) positioned beneath the action, glowing faintly when loaded
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: HELIX BIOSYSTEMS in sans-serif chrome lettering across the upper receiver. Circular molecular helix logo inlaid on the left side. Tiny serial placard (forensically registered) mounted on the underside of the stock. Medical-device regulation stamps embossed near the grip in gray.
physical_description.condition_typical: Typically well-maintained. Expensive enough to warrant armorer oversight. Field examples show minor scorching on the thermal vents and faint wear on the rubberized grip. No visible battle damage; if damaged, the weapon is decommissioned and recycled by Helix rather than field-repaired. Cosmetic scratches on the sapphire dish are common — the material is resilient but shows every contact.
